name: Neutral-Atom Arrays
what: Arrays of neutral atoms held by optical tweezers, notable for scaling to large qubit counts and flexible geometry.
how: Optical tweezers position atoms; Rydberg excitation creates strong, switchable interactions.

name: Superconducting Qubits
what: Qubits built from superconducting circuits cooled to near absolute zero, the most widely deployed quantum processor design today.
how: Josephson junctions form artificial atoms; microwave pulses drive gates inside a dilution refrigerator.

name: Trapped-Ion Qubits
what: Individual ions held in electromagnetic traps and manipulated with lasers, known for long coherence times and high gate fidelity.
how: Ions confined in RF traps; laser pulses drive entangling gates between any pair in the chain.

name: Photonic Quantum Computing
what: Quantum processors that encode information in light, able to operate without dilution refrigerators and integrate naturally with fibre networks.
how: Squeezed light states and interferometer meshes on photonic chips, measured with photon detectors.

name: Silicon Spin Qubits
what: Qubits encoded in the spin of single electrons in silicon, aiming to reuse existing semiconductor fabrication.
how: Gate-defined quantum dots in isotopically purified silicon, controlled electrically.

name: Topological Qubits
what: A qubit design that would store information non-locally so that local noise cannot corrupt it. Still unproven as a working processor.
how: Braiding of quasiparticle excitations in engineered superconductor–semiconductor devices.

name: Quantum Error Correction
use: Turning noisy qubits into reliable ones
what: Encoding one reliable logical qubit across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected mid-computation. The central obstacle between today's machines and useful ones.
how: Stabiliser codes such as the surface code, with repeated syndrome measurement and real-time decoding.

name: Logical Qubits
use: The unit that actually matters for applications
what: Error-corrected qubits assembled from many physical ones. Counting logical rather than physical qubits is the honest measure of a machine's power.
how: Error-correcting codes plus fault-tolerant gate schemes such as lattice surgery or transversal gates.

name: Real-Time Error Decoders
use: Keeping correction ahead of error accumulation
what: Classical hardware that interprets error syndromes fast enough to correct a running quantum computation, a prerequisite for fault tolerance.
how: FPGA and ASIC decoders running matching or neural-network algorithms within the qubit coherence window.

name: Magic State Distillation
what: A procedure to produce the high-quality resource states needed for the gates error-correcting codes cannot perform directly. A major driver of total qubit cost.
how: Many noisy resource states are consumed to distil fewer, cleaner ones.

name: Quantum Advantage Benchmarks
use: Measuring real progress against classical computers
what: Experiments claiming a quantum machine outperformed classical simulation on a specific task. Several have later been matched by improved classical algorithms, so each claim is provisional.
how: Random circuit sampling and boson sampling, checked against the best classical simulations.

name: Quantum Optimisation Algorithms
what: Algorithms that search for good solutions to hard combinatorial problems. Real-world advantage over the best classical methods remains unproven.
how: Variational circuits (QAOA) and quantum annealing schedules.

name: Quantum Simulation of Chemistry
what: Using quantum computers to model molecules and materials whose electron correlations are intractable classically — the application most experts expect to deliver value first.
how: Hamiltonian simulation and phase estimation on error-corrected hardware.

name: Shor's Algorithm
what: The algorithm that would break today's public-key cryptography by factoring large numbers efficiently. Requires far more error-corrected qubits than any machine now has.
how: Quantum period finding via the quantum Fourier transform.

name: Quantum Machine Learning
what: Machine-learning methods running on quantum hardware. Clearest theoretical benefit is for data that is itself quantum; claims of broad speedups on classical data are contested.
how: Parameterised quantum circuits trained with classical optimisers; quantum kernel methods.

name: Optical Atomic Clocks
what: Clocks referenced to optical atomic transitions, precise enough that relativistic time dilation is measurable over small height differences.
how: Ultra-stable lasers locked to narrow transitions in trapped atoms or ions.

name: Quantum Sensing
what: Measurement devices exploiting quantum states to beat classical sensitivity limits — the nearest-term commercial quantum technology.
how: Atom interferometers, NV-centre magnetometers and squeezed-light readout.

name: NV-Centre Magnetometry
what: Diamond defect centres used as magnetic-field sensors that work at room temperature and at very small scales.
how: Optically detected magnetic resonance of nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond.

name: Quantum Gravimetry
what: Gravity sensors using falling cold atoms, able to map buried structures and voids without excavation.
how: Atom interferometers measure acceleration of free-falling atomic clouds.

name: Quantum Key Distribution
what: Distributing encryption keys using quantum states, where interception disturbs the signal and is detected. Deployed on metro fibre links and satellite demonstrations.
how: Single-photon or continuous-variable protocols such as BB84 over fibre or free space.

name: Quantum Repeaters
use: Extending quantum links beyond fibre loss limits
what: Devices that extend entanglement across long distances without measuring the signal, the missing piece for a wide-area quantum network.
how: Entanglement swapping between memory nodes, with purification to restore fidelity.

name: Quantum Internet
what: A network distributing entanglement between distant quantum processors, enabling tasks no classical network can perform. Early multi-node testbeds exist; wide deployment does not.
how: Quantum memories, repeaters and entanglement-distribution protocols over fibre and satellite.

name: Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Risk
what: The risk that encrypted traffic captured today is stored until a future quantum computer can decrypt it — which makes migration urgent for data that must stay secret for years.
how: Mitigated by migrating long-lived secrets to post-quantum algorithms now.

name: Post-Quantum Cryptography
use: Protecting data against future quantum attack
what: Classical encryption algorithms designed to resist quantum attack, now standardised and being rolled out across major platforms — the practical response to Shor's algorithm.
how: Lattice-based, hash-based and code-based schemes selected through the NIST standardisation process.

name: Cryptographic Agility
what: Designing systems so encryption algorithms can be replaced quickly, so the next migration does not take a decade.
how: Abstracted crypto interfaces, inventory of cryptographic assets, hybrid classical/post-quantum modes.

name: Quantum Cloud Access
what: Cloud services giving remote access to quantum processors, how nearly all users reach quantum hardware today.
how: Job queues and SDKs over cloud APIs, often across several hardware vendors.

name: Quantum Software Stack
what: Compilers, transpilers and error-mitigation layers that turn an abstract algorithm into pulses a specific machine can run.
how: Circuit optimisation, qubit routing and hardware-aware scheduling.

name: Cryogenic Control Electronics
what: Control chips that operate inside the refrigerator, addressing the wiring problem that limits how many qubits a dilution fridge can host.
how: CMOS control ASICs qualified for millikelvin operation, multiplexing many qubit lines.

name: Surface-Code Error Correction
what: Two-dimensional lattices of physical qubits encode one logical qubit and correct both bit-flip and phase-flip errors, and several groups have now demonstrated logical error rates falling as the code distance grows. This crossing point is the threshold condition for scalable fault tolerance.
how: A square lattice of data and measure qubits is repeatedly interrogated by stabiliser measurements; a decoder infers the most likely error chain from the syndrome history and applies a correction.

name: Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
what: Quantum LDPC codes promise a tenfold or better reduction in the number of physical qubits needed per logical qubit compared with the surface code, by encoding information in highly connected high-rate codes. Small-scale demonstrations have already run on trapped-ion hardware.
how: Sparse parity-check matrices define a code whose stabilisers are measured on a connectivity graph; belief-propagation and ordered-statistics decoders recover the error pattern in near-linear time.

name: Quantum Error Mitigation
use: Extracting useful results from noisy hardware
what: Classical post-processing techniques suppress the effect of noise on near-term devices without full error correction, using zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation and symmetry verification. Mitigation buys usable accuracy today while correction matures.
how: Circuits are run at several noise levels and the results extrapolated to the zero-noise limit, or known noise channels are inverted statistically across many sampled circuit variants.

name: Variational Quantum Eigensolver
what: A hybrid approach in which a shallow parameterised quantum circuit prepares a trial state and a classical optimiser minimises its measured energy. It is the leading candidate for extracting chemistry value from pre-fault-tolerant hardware.
how: An ansatz circuit is executed on the quantum processor to measure expectation values of Pauli terms; a classical loop updates the parameters until the energy converges toward the ground state.

name: Quantum Phase Estimation
what: The canonical fault-tolerant primitive that reads out the eigenvalue of a unitary operator to arbitrary precision and underlies Shor factoring and quantum simulation. Its deep circuits make it the benchmark that error-corrected machines must clear.
how: An ancilla register is placed into superposition and controls repeated applications of the unitary to a target register; inverse quantum Fourier transform on the ancilla yields the phase as a binary fraction.

name: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Finance
use: Derivative pricing, risk analysis, portfolio optimisation
what: Amplitude estimation delivers a quadratic speedup over Monte Carlo sampling for expectation values, the core computation behind derivative pricing and risk aggregation. Banks are running the proof-of-concept work that will define first commercial advantage.
how: A state-preparation operator encodes the probability distribution and an objective operator marks favourable outcomes; amplitude estimation then extracts the expectation with quadratically fewer samples.

name: Optically Pumped Magnetometer MEG
use: Wearable brain imaging, epilepsy mapping, neuroscience
what: Atomic-vapour magnetometers detect the femtotesla magnetic fields of neuronal currents without cryogenics, allowing a helmet the patient can wear and move in. This replaces room-sized cryogenic SQUID arrays in clinical magnetoencephalography.
how: A rubidium vapour cell is optically pumped and probed by a detuned laser; the spin precession rate responds linearly to the ambient magnetic field, which is read optically.

name: Quantum Random Number Generator
use: Key generation, simulation, gaming, certified randomness
what: Devices that derive random bits from the intrinsic indeterminacy of quantum measurement produce randomness that is certified rather than assumed, unlike pseudorandom generators. Chip-scale units are already integrated into security modules and cloud services.
how: Single-photon detection events, vacuum fluctuations or phase noise in an optical interferometer are digitised and processed through a randomness extractor to yield unbiased output.

name: Cryogenic Dilution Refrigeration
use: Cooling superconducting and spin qubits to millikelvin temperatures
what: Dilution refrigerators are the enabling plant for superconducting and many semiconductor qubit platforms, holding mixing chambers below ten millikelvin for weeks. Throughput, wiring density and vibration isolation are now system-level constraints on qubit count.
how: Helium-3 and helium-4 are mixed and separated in a continuous cycle; the enthalpy of mixing across the phase boundary absorbs heat and cools the mixing chamber without moving parts in the cold stage.

name: Quantum Annealing
what: Special-purpose quantum processors that settle a network of qubits into a low-energy state encoding the answer to an optimisation problem, rather than running gate-based circuits.
how: Qubits start in superposition under a strong transverse field that is slowly reduced, letting the system settle toward the problem Hamiltonian ground state.

name: Grover's Algorithm
what: Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted space in square-root time, the canonical quadratic speedup underlying quantum approaches to unstructured search, constraint satisfaction and symmetric-key cryptanalysis.
how: An oracle marks the target state with a phase flip; repeated Grover iterations rotate amplitude toward the marked state, and after roughly the square root of N iterations a measurement returns the answer with high probability.

name: HHL Linear Systems Algorithm
what: The Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm solves sparse linear systems with exponential scaling advantage in the matrix dimension, the primitive behind many proposed quantum machine-learning and optimisation speedups.
how: Quantum phase estimation writes the matrix eigenvalues into an ancilla register; a controlled rotation inverts each eigenvalue and the register is uncomputed, leaving the solution vector encoded in the amplitudes of the system qubits.

name: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
what: QAOA is a variational near-term algorithm that approximates combinatorial optimisation problems as alternating cost and mixer operations on a gate-based device, without requiring full fault tolerance.
how: Parameters of the cost and mixer layers are tuned by a classical optimiser against measured expectation values; circuit depth and parameter choice trade solution quality against noise on the available hardware.

name: Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
what: Instead of executing a gate sequence, this model prepares a large entangled cluster state and computes by measuring its qubits one at a time, making it attractive for photonic hardware where two-qubit gates are probabilistic.
how: A cluster state is generated by entangling many qubits; adaptive single-qubit measurements with classical feed-forward of outcomes implement any circuit, consuming the entanglement as the computation proceeds.

name: Bosonic Cat Qubits
what: Qubits encoded in superpositions of coherent states of a microwave resonator are intrinsically biased against bit-flip errors, giving a hardware-level advantage that simplifies the error-correction stack.
how: A nonlinear element stabilises two coherent states of opposite phase inside the cavity; photon loss causes predominantly phase flips, so a cheap repetition code corrects the dominant error channel while bit flips remain exponentially suppressed.

name: Fluxonium Qubits
what: Fluxonium circuits trade the transmon's simple control scheme for much longer coherence times and larger anharmonicity, improving the fidelity of two-qubit gates and reducing leakage to higher levels.
how: A Josephson junction shunted by a large superinductance produces a heavy, well-localised wavefunction insensitive to charge noise, with transitions driven at lower frequencies than a comparable transmon.

name: GKP Bosonic Codes
what: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codes encode a logical qubit in a periodic grid of oscillator states, correcting both bit and phase flips within a single bosonic mode and enabling hardware-efficient error correction.
how: A microwave cavity is driven into a lattice of squeezed states; small displacement errors shift the lattice and are detected and corrected by measuring stabiliser displacements without collapsing the encoded logical information.

name: Quantum Memory
what: A quantum memory stores an unknown quantum state and releases it on demand with fidelity above the classical limit, the missing component for synchronising nodes in a quantum network.
how: Rare-earth-doped crystals or cold atomic ensembles absorb a photon into a collective excitation, hold it using spin echoes or dynamical decoupling, and re-emit it after a controllable delay.

name: Microwave-to-Optical Transduction
what: Superconducting qubits operate at microwave frequencies that attenuate rapidly in optical fibre, so a device converting single photons between microwave and telecom wavelengths is essential for linking quantum processors over distance.
how: Electro-optic or optomechanical devices couple a microwave cavity to an optical cavity so that a single microwave photon shifts the optical resonance, transferring the quantum state without adding thermal noise.
companies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

name: Quantum Illumination
what: Quantum illumination uses entangled photon pairs to detect a weakly reflecting target against a bright thermal background with fewer measurements than any classical radar operating at the same power.
how: One photon of each pair probes the target while its twin is retained locally; coincidence measurements between the returned and retained photons reveal the target even when the idler-target correlation is too faint to detect in either arm alone.

name: Squeezed-Light Interferometry
what: Injecting squeezed vacuum into a laser interferometer suppresses photon shot noise below the vacuum limit, directly extending the reach of gravitational-wave detectors into a larger volume of the universe.
how: A nonlinear optical parametric amplifier squeezes the phase-dependent uncertainty of the vacuum field; injecting it into the interferometer's dark port reduces noise in the measured quadrature at the cost of increased noise in the conjugate one.

name: Quantum-Enhanced Clock Networks
what: Linking optical clocks through fibre networks enables relativistic geodesy, searches for dark-matter couplings and a future redefinition of the second based on an optical transition.
how: Optical frequency combs convert clock signals to telecom wavelengths for fibre transport; comparing clocks at distant sites measures gravitational potential differences and slow drifts at centimetre and nanohertz sensitivity.
companies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

name: Quantum Control Electronics
what: Generating, timing and digitising the analogue signals that drive thousands of qubits is a scaling bottleneck second only to fabrication. Rack-mount and cryo-CMOS control stacks now target hundreds of channels per unit with picosecond synchronisation.
how: Arbitrary waveform generators and FPGAs synthesise microwave and baseband pulses, while digitising channels capture readout signals, all phase-locked to a shared reference clock.

name: Cold-Atom Gravimetry and Inertial Navigation
what: Cold-atom interferometers measure gravity and acceleration without the drift that limits classical instruments, which matters most where satellite navigation is unavailable. Instruments are already deployed for geophysical survey and are being ruggedised for vehicle use.
how: Atoms are cooled and launched, then split and recombined with laser pulses; the interference phase depends on the gravitational field difference along the two interferometer arms.
